answer: The premise is only partly right: both methods start from the adjacency matrix, so the difference lies in how they transform it, not in the information they access. Modularity (Tang & Liu) takes the top eigenvectors of the modularity matrix B = A - dd^T/(2m), which subtracts a degree-based null model. EdgeCluster instead runs k-means on edge-centric clustering of the adjacency structure. Modularity tends to outperform EdgeCluster when the graph has strong, assortative community structure that matches the labels (homophily), so the degree-corrected global spectral signal captures the relevant communities. It also tends to win when the number of embedding dimensions is modest and the graph is small to medium in size, where the eigendecomposition is feasible and the degree normalization removes hub bias. EdgeCluster tends to be competitive or better on very large, sparse networks where the eigendecomposition is too costly and an edge-level clustering scales more easily, or where community structure is weak and local edge patterns carry more of the label signal. These conditions are general patterns from the literature rather than a single definitive result, and the exact outcome depends on the dataset and evaluation setup.
